title: No. 71 — The Duration in Office of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Duration in office has been named as the second requisite of energy in the executive authority. It bears on two things: the personal firmness of the chief executive in using his constitutional powers, and the stability of the system of administration adopted under his leadership. As to the first, it must be evident that the longer the term in office, the greater the probability of gaining so important an advantage. It is a general principle of human nature that a man takes an interest in whatever he possesses in proportion to how secure or precarious his hold on it is. He will be less attached to what he holds by a momentary or uncertain title than to what he enjoys by a lasting and certain one, and he will naturally be willing to risk more for the one than for the other. This remark applies no less to a political privilege, honor or trust than to any ordinary article of property. The inference is that a man acting as chief executive, aware that in a very short time he MUST give up his office, will be apt to feel too little interest in it to risk any serious censure or difficulty by exerting his powers independently. He will not want to face the ill humors, however passing, that may prevail in a considerable part of society itself, or even in a dominant faction of the legislative body. Suppose instead that he MIGHT give up the office unless he is continued by a new choice, and that he wishes to be continued. Then his wishes, joining with his fears, would corrupt his integrity or debase his courage still more powerfully. In either case, feebleness and irresolution must be the marks of the office.

Some would be inclined to count the Executive's servile yielding to whatever current prevails, in the community or in the legislature, as its best recommendation. But such men hold very crude notions both of the purposes for which government was instituted and of the true means of promoting the public happiness. The republican principle demands that the deliberate sense of the community should govern the conduct of those to whom it entrusts the management of its affairs. It does not require unqualified compliance with every sudden breeze of passion, or with every passing impulse the people may receive from the arts of men who flatter their prejudices in order to betray their interests. It is a fair observation that the people commonly INTEND the PUBLIC GOOD. This is often true even of their errors. But their good sense would despise the flatterer who pretended that they always REASON RIGHT about the MEANS of promoting it. They know from experience that they sometimes err, and the wonder is that they err so seldom, constantly beset as they are by the wiles of parasites and sycophants, by the snares of the ambitious, the greedy and the desperate, and by the artifices of men who possess their confidence more than they deserve it, and of those who seek to possess it rather than deserve it. When occasions arise in which the interests of the people are at odds with their inclinations, it is the duty of the persons they have appointed as guardians of those interests to withstand the temporary delusion, so as to give the people time and opportunity for calmer and more sober reflection. Instances might be cited in which conduct of this kind has saved the people from the very fatal consequences of their own mistakes, and has won lasting monuments of their gratitude for the men who had the courage and magnanimity to serve them at the risk of their displeasure.

But however inclined we might be to insist on unbounded compliance in the Executive with the inclinations of the people, we cannot with any propriety insist on the same compliance with the whims of the legislature. The latter may sometimes stand in opposition to the former, and at other times the people may be entirely neutral. In either case it is certainly desirable that the Executive should be in a position to dare to act on his own opinion, with vigor and decision.

The same rule that teaches the propriety of a partition between the different branches of power also teaches that the partition should be arranged so as to make each independent of the others. What is the point of separating the executive or the judiciary from the legislative if both the executive and the judiciary are so constituted as to be at the absolute disposal of the legislative? Such a separation must be merely nominal, and unable to achieve the ends for which it was established. It is one thing to be subordinate to the laws and another to be dependent on the legislative body. The first is consistent with the fundamental principles of good government; the last violates them and, whatever the forms of the Constitution may be, unites all power in the same hands. The tendency of the legislative authority to absorb every other has been fully shown, with examples, in some earlier numbers. In governments that are purely republican, this tendency is almost irresistible. The representatives of the people in a popular assembly sometimes seem to fancy that they are the people themselves, and show strong signs of impatience and disgust at the least sign of opposition from any other quarter, as if the exercise of its rights by either the executive or the judiciary were a breach of their privilege and an outrage to their dignity. They often appear disposed to exert an imperious control over the other departments. And since they commonly have the people on their side, they always act with such momentum that it is very hard for the other members of the government to maintain the balance of the Constitution.

It may perhaps be asked how a short term in office can affect the independence of the Executive from the legislature, unless the one holds the power of appointing or removing the other. One answer to this question can be drawn from the principle already noted, namely the slight interest a man tends to take in a short-lived advantage, and the little inducement it gives him to expose himself to any considerable inconvenience or danger on its account. Another answer, perhaps more obvious though no more conclusive, comes from considering the influence of the legislative body over the people. That influence might be used to prevent the re-election of a man who, by honestly resisting some sinister project of that body, had made himself the target of its resentment.

It may also be asked whether a term of four years would serve the end proposed. If it would not, would a shorter period, which would at least be recommended by greater security against ambitious designs, not be preferable, for that reason, to a longer one that was still too short to inspire the firmness and independence wanted in the chief executive?

It cannot be asserted that a term of four years, or any other limited term, would completely serve the end proposed. But it would contribute toward it in a degree that would have a material influence on the spirit and character of the government. Between the beginning and the end of such a period there would always be a considerable interval in which the prospect of losing office would be far enough away not to affect improperly the conduct of a man with a fair share of fortitude. In that interval he might reasonably expect that there would be time enough, before the end arrived, to make the community aware of the propriety of the measures he was inclined to pursue. It is probable that as he approached the moment when the public were to express their judgment of his conduct by a new election, his confidence, and with it his firmness, would decline. Even so, both would draw support from the opportunities his earlier time in the office had given him to establish himself in the esteem and goodwill of his constituents. He could then take risks safely, in proportion to the proofs he had given of his wisdom and integrity, and to the claim he had earned to the respect and attachment of his fellow citizens. On the one hand, then, a term of four years will contribute enough to the firmness of the Executive to make it a very valuable ingredient in the composition. On the other hand, it is not enough to justify any alarm for public liberty. Consider the British House of Commons. From the most feeble beginnings, FROM THE MERE POWER OF ASSENTING OR DISAGREEING TO THE IMPOSITION OF A NEW TAX, it has by rapid strides reduced the prerogatives of the crown and the privileges of the nobility to the limits it judged compatible with the principles of a free government, while raising itself to the rank and consequence of a coequal branch of the legislature. In one instance it has been able to abolish both the royalty and the aristocracy and to overturn all the ancient establishments, in Church as well as State. On a recent occasion it has been able to make the monarch tremble at the prospect of an innovation(1) it attempted. If all this is so, what would be to be feared from an elective chief executive with a four-year term and the confined authorities of a President of the United States? Only that he might be unequal to the task the Constitution assigns him. I shall add only this: if his term is such as to leave a doubt about his firmness, that doubt is inconsistent with a jealousy of his encroachments.
1. This was the case with respect to Mr. Fox's India bill, which was carried in the House of Commons, and rejected in the House of Lords, to the entire satisfaction, as it is said, of the people.
